# A Skeptic's Guide to Cryptocurrency and Stablecoins

First listed: 2025-06-02 | Evaluation cutoff: 2026-11-10

[Back to library](../README.md)

## Source versions

- [YouTube: A Skeptic's Guide to Cryptocurrency and Stablecoins](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8NH_AZwsmCE) - 2025-06-02
- [Substack: A Skeptic's Guide to Cryptocurrency and Stablecoins](https://realeismanplaybook.substack.com/p/a-skeptics-guide-to-cryptocurrency-e99) - 2025-06-08

Earliest listed publication among matched versions, not proof of an unedited contemporaneous archive. Claim timestamps refer to the reviewed version.

## Summary

Eisman asks fintech strategist Rahul Jindal to explain why crypto should hedge monetary stress, how stablecoins work, and what they add to existing payment networks. He separates payment infrastructure from token speculation and presses the guest on switching costs, trust and Visa’s services. The dialogue also exposes confusion about Bitcoin divisibility, SOL versus stablecoins, and Visa+ reach. Jindal closes with crypto legislation and a preference for industry-specific payments software.

Eisman’s strongest contribution is the demand for a concrete use case, an observable thesis and an identified economic beneficiary. That framework is more defensible than several technical premises: the finite Bitcoin supply does not prevent fractional payments, Visa+ was not universal global app interoperability, and his 2023 market-loss chronology is wrong. Jindal’s near-term stablecoin-law prediction succeeded, while his year-end 2025 market-structure-law expectation missed. The guest’s momentary treatment of SOL as a dollar-backed stablecoin is explicitly separated from Eisman’s correction.

- [Bitcoin FAQ: supply, divisibility and fees](https://bitcoin.org/en/faq) (inspected 2026-11-10): The 21 million supply limit coexists with 100 million satoshis per bitcoin. Transaction fees depend on transaction size and congestion, not simply the value transferred.

<a id="youtube-8NH_AZwsmCE-c029"></a>
### 029. A dollar-reserve-backed stablecoin can be issued and redeemed against a corresponding dollar claim.

**Mixed** | Rahul Jindal | explanation | major

[Source at 22:30-23:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8NH_AZwsmCE&t=1350s) | Stance: asserted | Horizon: not stated

This describes a reserve-backed model, but a peg does not itself guarantee full reserves, frictionless redemption or every holder’s direct redemption rights. Other stablecoin designs differ.

Assessment test: Inspect the issuer agreement, assets, liabilities and redemption conditions.

- [Tether reserve-representation enforcement order](https://www.cftc.gov/PressRoom/PressReleases/8450-21) (2021-10-15): The order found misleading historical reserve representations and sufficient fiat reserves on only 27.6% of days in its 2016-18 sample. Historical misconduct does not establish current insolvency.
- [GENIUS Act, Public Law 119-27](https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/1582/text) (2025-07-18): Enacted July 18. The law permits qualifying state oversight at no more than $10 billion of outstanding issuance, with transition rules and waivers above the threshold. Federal regulator responsibilities depend on issuer type.

<a id="youtube-8NH_AZwsmCE-c030"></a>
### 030. Tether and Solana are comparable stablecoin exchanges or issuers.

**Wrong** | Steve Eisman | explanation | supporting

[Source at 23:37-24:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8NH_AZwsmCE&t=1417s) | Stance: corrected_in_dialogue | Horizon: not stated

This conflates issuer, blockchain and exchange. Tether issues USDT; Solana is a network on which tokens such as USDC can operate. The question drives a confused hypothetical.

Assessment test: Identify token, issuer, custodian, exchange and network separately.

- [Stablecoin payments](https://docs.stripe.com/payments/stablecoin-payments) (inspected 2026-11-10): Supported stablecoins and their networks are separate fields; USDC can run on Solana. Merchant payments can settle in local currency, support refunds, and lack ordinary dispute support.
- [Solana transaction fees](https://solana.com/docs/core/fees) (inspected 2026-11-10): Transaction fees are paid in SOL, with base and optional priority components. This is a protocol rule, not a forecast of SOL investment returns.
- [Tether reserve-representation enforcement order](https://www.cftc.gov/PressRoom/PressReleases/8450-21) (2021-10-15): The order found misleading historical reserve representations and sufficient fiat reserves on only 27.6% of days in its 2016-18 sample. Historical misconduct does not establish current insolvency.

## Framework and tools

- Separate a token investment, a stablecoin claim and the payment network that carries it.
- Ask what behavior the thesis predicts, while distinguishing a single trading day from a long-horizon hedge test.
- Compare total payment costs, fraud protection, settlement, refunds and switching costs.
- Check who earns reserve yield and who captures network economics.
- Prefer understandable businesses and test whether a new technology complements incumbents.
- Reserve quality and redemption rights matter more than the label stable.

Tools and charts discussed, not a complete visual inspection:

- Crypto/equity return correlation across regimes, with window and frequency specified.
- Reserve-backed token issuance, custody, redemption and reserve yield.
- Network fees versus issuer interchange and total merchant discount.
- Visa+, Visa Direct, stablecoin rails and cross-border remittance use cases.
- Legislative milestones and state/federal issuer-supervision thresholds.
- Industry-specific software, merchant retention and payment processing.
